figures.caption: Figure 7. Industrial image-AUROC/RAM trade-off across the selected industrial datasets. Each point reports macro image AUROC and the largest dataset-level peak RAM for one reported method or ablation.

Figure 3. Meniscus qualitative examples from the canonical streaming MH-PatchCore baseline. Each row shows one sample as the original image, anomaly-score heatmap overlay, and predicted segmentation overlay.

Figure 6. Meniscus RAM growth for original PatchCore and the selected GeoReS streaming trade-off. Original PatchCore improves by retaining more normal images, but its resident memory grows with the retained subset, whereas the bounded-memory construction stays near a fixed RAM band.

Table 5. Industrial Meniscus reduced-data comparison. Each block uses the same fixedseed normal-training subset and compares original PatchCore with the canonical streaming baseline and the selected streaming memory–accuracy tradeoff used in the RAM-growth plot. Peak RAM is reported in GB, fit time in seconds, and inference latency in milliseconds per image; lower is better for telemetry.
Table 15. MVTec AD per-category peak resident memory. The final rows report the mean and maximum of the category-level peaks. Values are reported in GB; lower is better.
Table 2. Configuration summary for the main method comparisons and targeted controls. The rows define the contrasts used in the reported accuracy–resource results.

Figure 2. Conceptual comparison between the offline PatchCore baseline and the streaming covariance-aware variant studied in this paper. The diagram contrasts the point at which the support set is built and the geometry used for nearest-neighbour retrieval.
Table 18. Industrial peak resident memory on the selected industrial datasets. The final rows report the mean and maximum of the dataset-level peaks. Values are reported in GB; lower is better.

Table 10. MVTec AD category-wise k-center budget ablation in AUROC. The comparison is anchored by the canonical streaming baseline. Each cell reports image-level AUROC and, in parentheses, pixel-level AUROC. The vertically separated Original PatchCore column is an offline reference and is excluded from boldface selection.

Figure 5. Lyo qualitative examples from the canonical streaming MH-PatchCore baseline. Each row shows one sample as the original image, anomaly-score heatmap overlay, and predicted segmentation overlay.
Table 16. MVTec AD per-category per-image inference time. The final row reports the image-weighted mean across all test images. Values are reported in ms/image; lower is better.

Table 11. MVTec AD category-wise GeoReS ablation in AUROC. Each cell reports image-level AUROC and, in parentheses, pixel-level AUROC. The vertically separated Original PatchCore column is an offline reference and is excluded from boldface selection.

Table 1. Benchmark and industrial datasets used in the evaluation protocol. MVTec AD is expanded by category because each category defines a separate one-class anomalydetection dataset. The “Anom. eval” column reports the anomalous labels entering metric computation; for MVTec AD this follows the fixed image–mask preprocessing used for pixel-aware evaluation, and for the industrial datasets it follows the image-level test labels.

Figure 4. Bottom qualitative examples from the canonical streaming MH-PatchCore baseline. Each row shows one sample as the original image, anomaly-score heatmap overlay, and predicted segmentation overlay.

Table 13. Industrial dataset-wise GeoReS ablation in AUROC. Values are image-level AUROC. The vertically separated Original PatchCore column is an offline reference and is excluded from boldface selection.
